name: Leo Tolstoy
role: Russian novelist and Christian pacifist and anarchist thinker (1828-1910)
summary: From the 1880s Tolstoy held that Christ's teaching forbids all violence and so rules out the state, the army, courts, prisons and taxes, which he saw as organised violence that enslaves workers. He condemned private property in land and rent, interest and wages, backed Henry George's land tax, rejected revolution and parliamentary reform alike, and called patriotism a fraud. He urged simple living, vegetarianism, chastity and a religion of love freed from Church dogma.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Bethink Yourselves! rejects war as such, defensive wars included, so armed force for further purposes is excluded.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: Thou Shalt Not Kill condemns all killing, in war and by governments, as murder; killing civilians is not exempt.

religious-offensive-war.rationale: He rejects all war and all killing, and Bethink Yourselves! says Christ's name may not be taught by force, so war to spread a faith is excluded.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: A Letter to a Hindu urges Indians to resist British rule by refusing to serve and cooperate and not by force, since violence breeds more violence.

remove-indigenous-peoples.rationale: Patriotism and Government condemns the scramble to seize other peoples' lands in Asia, Africa and America, and he rejects the violence that removal needs.

remove-other-ethnic-groups-from-country.rationale: He calls national exclusivity a fraud incompatible with the brotherhood of peoples (Patriotism and Government), and rejects the violence expulsion needs (Thou Shalt Not Kill).

recognize-territorial-claims-from-conque.rationale: Patriotism and Government condemns the competition to seize other peoples' territory as the work of governments.

divinely-chosen-superior-people.rationale: What I Believe contrasts Christ's doctrine, open to all, with the Jewish belief in a chosen people, and Patriotism and Government rejects any claim that one people is best.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: The Gospel in Brief, his own rendering of the gospels, says one may choose to have no wife but may not take more than one, since a second wife breaks God's will.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: The First Step calls the use of animals for food immoral because it requires killing and says flesh food is unnecessary.

physical-labour-duty.rationale: What Then Must We Do? makes bread labour, one's own manual work, a duty of everyone who eats, and calls on the educated to take it up.

legal-duty-to-work.rationale: He holds that government law rests on organised violence and should be abolished (The Slavery of Our Times), so a legal compulsion to work is excluded.

labour-priority-over-capital.rationale: What Then Must We Do? argues that income should come from one's own work and that rent and interest on capital are unjust.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: What Then Must We Do? calls hired wages, with rent and interest, an unjust means of living on others' labour and describes free communes without them.

unions-run-economy.rationale: The Slavery of Our Times says workers should not look for change through unions, parliament or government, and he rejects any governing apparatus over the economy.

workers-parties-campaign-reforms.rationale: The Slavery of Our Times says workers should not seek change through unions, parties or parliament, and that reform legislation only legalises new slavery.

parliamentary-road-socialism.rationale: He rejects parliaments as a way out of slavery (The Slavery of Our Times) and says constitutions and parliamentary reform will not bring deliverance (Bethink Yourselves!).

constitutional-jury-trial.rationale: What I Believe says compulsory jury service forces a Christian into condemning others, contrary to Christ's commandments, and he rejects courts as violence.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: He holds that the state rests on organised violence and should be abolished (The Slavery of Our Times), so a state that sets and supports a way of life is excluded.

power-shapes-accepted-knowledge.rationale: The Slavery of Our Times treats learned economists and jurists as new priests who prove that the existing order is right, and What Is Art? says the upper classes' art serves them.

students-direct-own-learning.rationale: In his essays on education he objects that school discipline forbids children to ask questions or choose their subjects and argues for freer schools.

abolish-income-tax.rationale: The Slavery of Our Times says taxes are imposed by force and not by consent, and that people should refuse them; he does not single out income tax.

criminalize-genocide-denial.rationale: He condemns state censorship and prosecution of opinion (preface to What Is Art?, To the Tsar and His Assistants), and criminal penalties are state violence he rejects.

democracy-becomes-oligarchy.rationale: The Slavery of Our Times says elections, like inheritance, do not put the best in power, and The Kingdom of God Is Within You says men in authority, however chosen, are corrupt.

Themes searched in the texts: government and the state, war and patriotism, nation and empire, property, land and tax, money and wages, socialism and revolution, religion and church-state, marriage and sex, animals, technology, censorship, education and language, courts and juries, conscription, arbitration, civil disobedience. No position was found on healthcare, minimum wage, trade, central banking, immigration, gender, race and LGBT questions or other modern policy matters, so those are null. Several answers (state functions, armed forces, police, legal compulsion) come from his explicit rejection of violence and of the state, not from comments on the specific policy, and are medium. I Cannot Be Silent was read in the Wikisource transcription.
